title: Staying with the trouble
author: Chris Mowles
summary: Chris Mowles, a complexity scholar, begins with Sherry Turkle's argument that AI companions train us toward passivity and experience-avoidance, then widens it into a critique of the instrumentalised thinking that pervades organisational life. He sets two events side by side: his research group's baggy, conversational annual conference and a tightly timed facilitated workshop in which he felt 'facilitated from pillar to post'. The second assumed that meaningful talk requires every minute to be structured, a process to have a process. He answers Mike Jackson's preference for more structure by arguing that sometimes going nowhere is the point, because the way a group handles its dilemmas is itself data. For problems that are political and social rather than technical, containing uncertainty with pre-reflected methods may erode the capacity for new thought. His closing question is whether the methods we build against uncertainty are what reduce our capacity to become ourselves, a challenge for leaders who over-engineer meetings.
points: Turkle's warning that AI relationships remove friction and surprise is used as a lens on organisations that also try to remove friction from how people meet.
A conference with only fixed start and finish times, a keynote and open conversation was the highlight of many delegates' year, while a fully timed workshop left Mowles with no moment to reflect.
Wrapping every meeting in structure, a 'process to have a process', prizes conformity to the task and squeezes out the spontaneous and the ability to affect and be affected.
Where problems are political and social rather than technical, how a group currently handles its dilemmas is the most useful data, so apparent time-wasting can be productive.
Methods designed as a hedge against uncertainty may be what diminish human resourcefulness, whether through AI or through over-schematic facilitation.
quotes: They are training us to be more passive, more dependent, and experience-avoidant.
Turkle argues that we are moving from an attention economy to an attachment economy.

The aim is often to make meetings more ‘effective and efficient’, to make maximum use of our precious time together, but perhaps also to render them friction-free and more predictable. For me this is the same kind of instrumentalised thinking that informs AI.
It’s a baggy, sometimes frustrating, sometimes conflictual affair where the dynamics of inclusion and exclusion play out all weekend, and where many delegates say it’s the highlight of their year.

I am sure the day produced some good ideas, and was helpful to the sponsors of the event, but I felt facilitated from pillar to post. There was never a moment to reflect; I got to know no one in the room

It was a process to have a process which valued conformity to the task, clearing away any friction: all we had to do was obey. For me it squeezed out the uncertain, the spontaneous, the ability to affect and be affected.
Sometimes going nowhere is the point because it offers something else to notice and to think and talk about.

Is it a possibility that it is the very methods we have developed as a hedge against uncertainty, against wasting our time, that reduce our capacity to become ourselves, whether it’s through the take up of AI, or schematics we use to tackle our problems?
